common_name: Compacta Neoregelia (Dwarf Punctatissima Bromeliad, Compact Blushing Bromeliad)

planting.note: Move potted offsets outdoors once nights stay reliably above 55°F, and bring plants back under cover before the first fall frost since foliage damages quickly below freezing.

directions: This dwarf selection of Neoregelia punctatissima forms a tight rosette of yellow-green leaves banded in maroon, staying noticeably smaller than the species type and well suited to container culture on a patio or deck. Give it bright, filtered light rather than harsh midday sun on the Gulf Coast, since intense reflected heat can scorch the thin leaf margins even though the genus tolerates more sun than most bromeliads. Keep the central cup topped off with water and flush it out periodically so it doesn't stagnate, and grow it in a coarse, fast-draining bark or bromeliad mix rather than garden soil. In zone 9a treat it strictly as a warm-season container accent, bringing it indoors or into a greenhouse whenever nights threaten to dip near freezing.
sources: Bird Rock Tropicals bromeliad growing guide

common_name: Tiger Neoregelia (Tigrina Bromeliad, Tiger-Striped Blushing Bromeliad)

planting.note: Set stoloniferous offsets or mounted pups outdoors after the last frost date and bring them back under cover before the first freeze of fall.

directions: Native to Brazil, this small, stoloniferous species produces flaring yellow-green leaves marked with fine burgundy tiger-striping and pure white flowers sunk into the central cup. Its wandering stolons let it spread into a colony over a season, making it a good candidate for mounting on driftwood or hanging baskets rather than a single pot. Give it bright, dappled light — enough to intensify the tiger markings without the scorching that full Gulf Coast summer sun can cause on such thin-leaved forms. Keep the cup filled with fresh water, use an open bark-based potting mix, and treat it as a warm-season patio or shade-house plant that must come indoors before frost in zone 9a.
sources: Encyclopedia of Bromeliads (Florida Council of Bromeliad Societies)

common_name: Perfection Bromeliad (Fosperior Perfection Neoregelia, Burgundy-Cupped Blushing Bromeliad)

planting.note: Move container-grown offsets outside for the warm season once night temperatures stay above 55°F, returning them indoors before the first fall frost.

directions: Bred by Bert Foster and long considered a benchmark hybrid in the bromeliad hobby, 'Perfection' forms a broad, symmetrical rosette with green-edged leaves that deepen to rich burgundy toward the central cup. It reaches a larger, more architectural size than many patio Neoregelias, making a strong specimen planting for a shaded courtyard container or an accent bed under high tree canopy. Strong filtered light brings out the best color contrast between the green margins and burgundy centers, while too much deep shade will fade the coloring to plain green. Keep the central vase filled with fresh water, use a coarse, well-drained bark or bromeliad mix, and protect it from any temperature near freezing, since it has no frost tolerance in a zone 9a landscape.

common_name: Charm Bromeliad (Maroon-Spotted Blushing Bromeliad, Marmorata Hybrid Neoregelia)

planting.note: Set potted offsets outdoors for the warm season after the last frost, and move them back under cover before nighttime temperatures approach freezing in fall.

directions: Registered hybrid bred to combine the broad, rounded form of Neoregelia marmorata with the bold maroon spotting of N. chlorosticta, 'Charm' produces a green rosette heavily blotched and patched with deep maroon that intensifies with bright, indirect light. It works equally well mounted on a piece of wood or grown in a shallow container of coarse, fast-draining bromeliad mix, and its moderate size fits nicely on a patio table or garden bench as a season-long focal point. Keep the central cup topped with water year-round and flush it occasionally to prevent stagnation, and avoid harsh midday sun that can bleach or scorch the patterned foliage in Gulf Coast heat. In zone 9a it is strictly a warm-weather outdoor plant that must be brought inside before frost.

common_name: Windii Queen's Tears (Billbergia x windii, Pink-Bracted Queen's Tears Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide and pot offsets in spring, moving clumps outdoors to a sheltered spot once hard freezes have passed; clumps left in the ground in zone 9a should be mulched heavily or moved to containers over winter.

directions: A classic hybrid between Billbergia nutans and B. decora, 'Windii' inherits the cold-hardiness of Queen's Tears along with the larger, showier pink bracts of its decora parent, making its pendant late-winter flower spikes more dramatic than the straight species. It forms loose, arching clumps of narrow gray-green leaves that spread readily by offsets, so it fills a hanging basket or wide container quickly and can also be massed as a shaded groundcover in protected Gulf Coast beds. It tolerates more neglect and drought than most bromeliads and needs only an occasional deep watering and light feeding to keep multiplying. In a 9a landscape it is among the more freeze-tolerant tank bromeliads, often surviving brief light frosts in a sheltered spot when its central cups are protected from standing ice.

common_name: Blue Rain Bromeliad (Blue Rain Aechmea, Purple-Flowered Tank Bromeliad)

planting.note: Move container plants outdoors for the warm season once nights stay reliably above 55°F, and bring them back inside well before the first fall frost.

directions: This hybrid tank bromeliad forms a rosette of glossy, strap-shaped green leaves topped in summer by a red flower stem carrying an arching spike of deep violet-blue blooms that hold their color for weeks before ripening into red berries. Grow it in a coarse, free-draining bark or orchid-style mix rather than potting soil, since its small root system needs excellent aeration and depends mainly on the central cup for moisture and nutrients. Bright, filtered light keeps the foliage compact and encourages strong bloom spikes, while deep shade produces a looser, less floriferous rosette. As a patio accent in zone 9a it thrives outdoors through the humid Gulf Coast summer but has no cold tolerance, so it must be moved under cover whenever a freeze threatens.
